content: Section X of the document, titled Lorem Ipsum: An Integration Resource Guide for Immunization Services Throughout the Life Course, provides a comprehensive framework for integrating immunization services with other health interventions across various stages of life. The guide emphasizes collaboration and integration as key strategies to strengthen health systems and improve service delivery. The World Health Organization (WHO) published this guide in 2018 under the ISBN 978-92-4-151473-6. The document is distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing users to copy, redistribute, and adapt the content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If the work is translated, a disclaimer must be included, stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guide is intended for national managers of immunization, reproductive, maternal, child, and adolescent health programs, as well as global, regional, and country-level policymakers and partners involved in designing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating integrated health services. Its objectives include encouraging program managers to explore opportunities for integration, summarizing global policies and strategies related to immunization integration, and providing planning resources, including a checklist to assess the suitability of programs for integration. It also aims to support the effective design, implementation, and evaluation of integrated immunization programs while addressing local contexts and highlighting knowledge gaps to encourage further research. The guide is structured to provide an overview of integration and its importance for immunization, followed by types of integration and health services that could provide immunization services or referrals. It includes a section on planning integrated immunization programs, discussing criteria such as context, compatibility, feasibility, acceptability, accountability, and equity. Another section focuses on monitoring and evaluating integrated health services, emphasizing the need to improve understanding of what works and what does not in integration efforts. The benefits and risks of integration are also discussed, along with useful references and considerations for integrating specific interventions with immunization. WHO defines integrated health services as those managed and delivered to ensure individuals receive a continuum of health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, disease management, rehabilitation, and palliative care services, coordinated across different levels and sites of care within and beyond the health sector, according to their needs throughout the life course. The guide highlights the growing importance of integration in health systems and immunization programs, as reflected in global policies and strategies. Routine immunization has a history of integration with other programs, such as vitamin A supplementation, growth monitoring, deworming, and insecticide-treated bed nets. Integration is seen as a continuum rather than a binary state, with varying degrees of integration across programs. The life course approach to immunization, as recommended in the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) and the Global Routine Immunization Strategies and Practices (GRISP), focuses on addressing population health needs over time. This approach provides additional opportunities for integrating age-appropriate interventions, improving coverage, efficiency, and cost-sharing, and reducing missed opportunities for vaccination. Integration is particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings, where it can enhance the efficiency of health service delivery. The guide also includes summaries of relevant studies, documented country experiences, and links to additional references. It is not intended to be a systematic review of evidence but rather a resource guide for policymakers and program managers. The appendix outlines specific interventions that can be integrated with immunization, such as nutrition, growth monitoring, malaria prevention, neglected tropical diseases, reproductive and maternal health services, HIV services, and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions. In summary, this resource guide serves as a practical tool for integrating immunization services with other health interventions, strengthening health systems, and addressing population health needs throughout the life course.
